Knoxville TN web design for businesses on the road to the Smokies

Some of your customers live in Fountain City. Some are passing through on the way to Gatlinburg. A good site talks to both, and you can see yours free before paying.

Knoxville TN web design has an unusual job: the same business often sells to two crowds who never meet. One crowd lives here and shops in Bearden, Fountain City and Farragut all year. The other is driving through on the way to the mountains, searching on a phone at a gas pump for a guide, a rental, a meal or someone to clean the cabin before the next family checks in. A site that only speaks to one of them leaves money on the table.

Dominion Web Design Pro writes sites that speak to both. Maurice Johnson builds every page by hand from Big Sandy in East Texas, shows you a free demo of your own site first, and charges one printed price.

The busiest national park sits just over the hill

Great Smoky Mountains National Park recorded about 11.5 million visits in 2025, the most of any national park and more than twice the count at Zion, which came second. Most of those visitors pass near Knoxville on their way in or out, and plenty of them need something on the way.

The money is real. State tourism figures put 2024 visitor spending in Sevier County, home to Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg, at about $3.93 billion, third among Tennessee's 95 counties. Tennessee as a whole counted 147 million visitors and $31.66 billion in direct visitor spending that year.

For a Knoxville owner that means two kinds of searches hit the same website. A visitor types "kayak rental near Knoxville" from a hotel room on a Thursday night. A homeowner in West Knoxville types "landscaper Bearden" on a Saturday morning. Both expect an answer in a few seconds, and both leave if they cannot find the hours or the phone number.

One week in the life of a cabin turnover crew

This is an example, not a client: a made-up two-person cleaning business based in South Knoxville, to show where a website earns its keep.

  1. Monday: the property manager checks you outA rental manager with cabins near Pigeon Forge needs a backup crew. She searches, finds three companies and opens each site. She wants to see the area you cover, whether you do linens and restocking, and how to reach you the same day.
  2. Wednesday: the owner from out of stateSomeone who owns one cabin and lives in Ohio searches at night. He cannot meet you. Your site is the whole interview, so it needs your name, what a turnover includes and a form that lands in your inbox.
  3. Friday: the local clientA family in Fountain City wants a deep clean before company comes. They searched for house cleaning, not cabins. A separate page for residential work is how they find you.
  4. Sunday night: checking messagesEvery lead from the week sits in one email folder, with a name and a number, because the contact form sent each one there.

What visitors need from the page that locals do not

A person from Atlanta or Cincinnati does not know how far Maryville is from downtown or how long the drive to the park entrance takes. They do not know your shop closes early on Sundays. So the site has to say it: where you are in plain terms, the hours by season if they change, whether to book ahead, and what to bring. Outfitters and guides should answer the questions they hear at the counter every day, on the page, before anyone has to call.

Locals want different things. They want proof you are still in business, the neighborhoods you cover and a way to get a quote without a long phone call. Writing one page for both readers usually fails both. Writing a page for each kind of customer, and a page for each service, works better and gives Google a clearer picture of what you do.

Knoxville TN web design that knows the neighborhoods

Customers describe Knoxville by the part of town they live in, and a page that uses those names reads like it was written by someone who asked. Here is how a few of them shape what a site should say.

PlaceWhat is going on thereWhat your page should mention
Market SquareLaid out in 1854 as a market for regional farmers and listed on the National Register in 1984. Its shopkeepers over the years included German, Swiss, Jewish and Greek immigrants, and it still draws crowds for events such as the spring Chalk Walk.Walking directions, parking, event-day hours.
Gay Street and the Old CityGay Street has been the main commercial street since the 1790s. When the 1919 viaduct raised the street, many businesses moved their front doors up a floor. The Old City is known for nightlife and live music.Which entrance, which floor, late hours.
South KnoxvilleThe city says the Urban Wilderness South Loop connects more than 60 miles of trails, built with Legacy Parks Foundation, Knox County, Ijams Nature Center and local mountain bikers.Trail access, bike or gear services, parking near trailheads.
Bearden, Fountain City, FarragutEstablished residential areas where people hire for homes and families.The streets and subdivisions you serve, quote forms, response times.
MaryvilleA separate city from Knoxville, with customers who search its own name.A page of its own if you work there, not a town name pasted in a list.

Google says local results depend mostly on relevance, distance and prominence. Prominence takes time to build through reviews and mentions. Relevance you can fix this month: a page that names the job and the place gives Google something specific to match. We do not promise rankings, because nobody honest can. We do write pages that are plainly about your work in the places you name.

Labs, a flagship campus and the vendors who serve them

Not every Knoxville customer is a tourist or a homeowner. Oak Ridge National Laboratory, in nearby Oak Ridge, is the largest science and energy lab in the Department of Energy system, and the University of Tennessee works with the lab through a long partnership while running its own large campus in Knoxville. Both run on a long tail of small suppliers: electricians, caterers, printers, movers, IT help, cleaning contracts and consultants.

Those buyers check a vendor out online before they call. They look for what you do, who you have the capacity to serve, any licenses your trade requires, and a real way to reach you. If you searched for web development Knoxville firms because you need more than a brochure, the honest answer is that a clear, fast, well-written site covers most of what these buyers want. Custom software is a different project, and we will tell you if that is what you need.

We do not sell page counts. A business that serves Knoxville, Maryville and the Sevier County cabins needs a strong page for each, not a hundred thin ones.

Common questions

What should Knoxville website design include for a business that serves tourists?

Put the things a visitor cannot guess on the first screen: where you are relative to the route they are driving, the hours for this season, whether they need to book ahead, and a phone number that dials with one tap. Add a page for each service, like guided trips, gear rental or cabin turnovers, so each one can be found on its own search. Locals need the same clarity, plus the parts of town you cover.

How do I choose a Knoxville web design company?

Ask for the total price in writing, who owns the domain and the finished site, what monthly fees follow launch, and who will actually write your pages. Then ask to see something built for a business like yours. Dominion Web Design Pro answers the first questions on this page: $497, $997 or $1,997 one time, you own the site, and Maurice Johnson writes it himself. The free demo covers the last one.

Do you offer web development in Knoxville, or only design?

We build complete small business sites: designed, written, coded, connected to a contact form that emails you every lead, and set up with titles, descriptions, a sitemap and schema for search. We do not build online stores or custom software such as a reservation engine tied to your own database. If your outfitting or rental business needs a booking system, tell us when you ask for the demo and we will say plainly what we can and cannot do.

Can one site cover Knoxville, Maryville and Sevier County?

Yes, and it should if you work in all three. The Pro package includes ten city pages, each researched and written about one place, so a pressure washing crew in Farragut can have a page for Maryville that says something true about Maryville. Agency starts with keyword research across your whole area and builds a page for each town and service pair that research supports.

How much does web design in Knoxville, TN cost?

Local quotes range from cheap builder plans to agency projects in the thousands, and many firms only quote after a call. Ours are printed: Starter is $497 for five pages, Pro is $997 for ten pages plus ten city pages and local SEO setup, and Agency is $1,997 for a research-led build. Hosting, maintenance and updates are $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent.

See your website before you pay for it

Give us your business name and what you do, and a demo site gets built for you to look at on your own phone. If you like it, pick a package. If you do not, you have spent nothing but the minute it took to look.
